messages.author: d1237c2d244e29ff
messages.subject: CES Estimation in Stan
parts:
I'd like to fit a variant of the CES function in Stan. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_elasticity_of_substitution

Q[i] = F (a K[i]^r +(1-a) L[i]^r)^(1/r)

where:
  r ∈ (-1,0)U(0,∞)
  a ∈ (0,1)
  F ∈ (0,∞)

And Q, K and L are >0 data.

The parameter, r, has support over the union of the open continuous interval from -1 to 0, and the positive reals. There is, however, an undefined point at zero, which leads to a divergent gradiant warning when I initialize at zero. The model runs when initialized at different values, but I am wondering if the pole at zero leads to abnormal behavior in Stan more generally. Any ideas? Is there a way to define the constraints than <lower=-1>?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: CES Estimation in Stan
parts:
I think you will be okay as long as you don't initialize it to exactly zero. Or you could fill in the discontinuity at r = 0 with a Cobb-Douglas function. The derivative is smooth through zero so I think NUTS will be able to pass over it without experiencing the problems we sometimes see with abs() or piecewise functions.

Ben

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: CES Estimation in Stan
parts:
If you have prior knowledge about parameter r being positive or negative, I would use that to define the support (restrict to either positive or negative).

If you don't know this, you may consider defining two separate parameters real r_pos<lower=0> and real r_neg<lower=-1, upper=0>, calculate and temporarily store the log-posterior for each (using all the data), and then mix the two with to-be-estimated mixing weights real W_neg<lower=0,upper=1> and 1-W_neg. If you run into trouble because r_pos or r_neg is pulled towards zero, you can add some soft constraints using a prior with zero density at zero.

messages.author: d1237c2d244e29ff
messages.subject: Re: CES Estimation in Stan
parts:
Thanks for the advice. I think I might just declare that r>0 be fiat. It is what the data suggest anyways.

The mixing idea is nice, but my model is too big to fit twice.

It would be interesting to see Stan behaves in some simply test cases with these kinds of models more generally.

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: CES Estimation in Stan
parts:
Ok sounds like a plan.

In this case, the model being big should not be a problem for a mixture model. It would only cost you double time (for having two mixture components) and a bit extra for the calculation of constant terms that are normally dropped when using statements based on "~". If you specify a local variable in the model section to store the total log-probability of all data given one of the r-parameters, you can just increment that variable by looping through your data (or units of data if things are vectorized). At the end, you only need to use log_sum_exp once to mix the two log-probabilties. What problems do you anticipate?
